title.en: Venezuela faces a deepening energy crisis as protests grow
title.vi: Venezuela đối mặt với khủng hoảng năng lượng trầm trọng khi biểu tình bùng phát

hook.en: For residents of Maracaibo, one of Venezuela’s largest and most economically important cities, the crisis has become deeply personal. Yanira says she can spend at least six hours a day without electricity. The outages have affected both her livelihood and her mental health.
hook.vi: Đối với cư dân Maracaibo, một trong những thành phố lớn và có tầm quan trọng kinh tế hàng đầu Venezuela, cuộc khủng hoảng đã trở nên vô cùng cá nhân. Yanira cho biết cô có thể dành ít nhất [y:sáu tiếng một ngày] không có điện. Những đợt cúp điện đã ảnh hưởng đến cả sinh kế lẫn sức khỏe tinh thần của cô.

sections.body_en:
She has had a hard time finding a job or even working remotely, because blackouts make it difficult to function. She eventually began running small businesses from home, first selling sandwiches and cepillados zulianos — shaved-ice treats popular in the region — but keeping food frozen and drinks cold is a constant challenge when electricity can disappear without warning:

The hardest moments come at night. Without air conditioning, sleeping becomes difficult in Maracaibo’s intense heat — and while opening the windows brings some relief, it also lets tropical insects inside. Yanira says the situation has affected her sleep so severely that she began taking sleeping pills.

Her experience reflects a broader problem. According to Venezuela’s 2025 Living Conditions Survey, only around [y:10 percent] of Venezuelans live without experiencing power outages. For most of the population, unreliable electricity has become a chronic part of daily life.

The blackouts are also taking a toll on local economies. The National Chamber of Commerce reported that [y:38 percent of businesses had closed] during the year, amid the combined effects of the electricity crisis and the country’s broader economic difficulties.

In Puertos de Altagracia which, like Maracaibo, is situated in Zulia state, Sara Hernández works at a company that sells bottled drinking water. Even with access to a generator, keeping the business running during outages is difficult because fuel is not always available. The uncertainty makes planning almost impossible. Electricity can disappear at any moment, and some businesses experience more than one rationing period in a single day.

The consequences extend beyond commerce. In Maracay, in Venezuela’s central region, resident Kellys Gallardo told El País that she receives daily text messages from the state electricity company, Corpoelec, warning her about planned outages, but the messages sometimes arrive only after the power has been cut.

Gallardo, who works at a company that manufactures printer ink cartridges, experiences outages both at work and at home. Her children are also affected when electricity rationing disrupts their schools.

As blackouts grow longer and less predictable, anger is becoming increasingly visible in public spaces. Residents who once endured outages quietly are now gathering in the streets, blocking roads and demanding solutions. In cities like Turmero, Valencia, El Tocuyo, Caja Seca, Calabozo, Zaraza and Valle de la Pascua, nighttime protests have highlighted how deeply the electricity crisis has entered everyday life.

The year 2026 saw a significant surge in both the frequency and widespread nature of civil unrest across Venezuela. The Observatorio Venezolano de Conflictividad Social (OVCS) documented [y:upwards of 4,000 protests] between January and August, a figure that OVCS coordinator Marco Antonio Ponce noted is triple the amount seen in earlier comparable timeframes. Daily demonstrations averaged 22 in August alone, with persistent electricity blackouts ranking among the public’s primary grievances.

For Venezuelans, the problem is about more than having to sit in the dark. It means businesses losing products and working hours, children having no electricity at school, families struggling to sleep in extreme heat, workers unable to plan their days, and people unable to access healthcare. In the Barquisimeto dialisis unit, for example, a lack of power left 42 kidney patients without treatment.

sections.heading_en: A problem that has lasted for years
sections.body_en:
Venezuela’s current electricity emergency echoes its 2019 crisis, when severe drought reduced water levels at the Guri reservoir, the hydroelectric complex that supplies a major share of the country’s electricity. One the most important events of this period was a 6six-day national blackout.

Today’s crisis is unfolding on top of years of deterioration in the electricity system. Venezuela has an installed generation capacity of approximately 30,000 megawatts, but currently produces [y:less than half] of that amount. The gap becomes particularly problematic during periods of high demand.

The government recently announced new investments aimed at rebuilding the system. In June, authorities signed an agreement with U.S.-based General Electric to restore 1,000MW of generating capacity over two years, with plans for an additional 5,000MW over the following four years.

Another agreement involving the Tocoma hydroelectric project, which began construction in 2007 but was never completed, was also announced. Authorities say these projects form part of a broader effort to recover Venezuela’s electricity infrastructure.

For residents living through the outages, however, long-term plans offer little immediate relief. In a country where electricity shortages have persisted for years, each new blackout carries the weight of a much longer story: one in which an essential public service has become increasingly unreliable, while residents are left waiting for the lights to come back on.

origin.originalTitle: Venezuela faces a deepening energy crisis as protests grow
changes: key point and apply steps added

keyPoint.en: Living through a severe energy crisis is like trying to build a house on a shifting foundation, where every routine task becomes a frustrating obstacle. How can you better prepare your household for sudden disruptions in essential public services? [p:Establishing a flexible daily routine] can help you adapt when infrastructure fails.
keyPoint.vi: Sống qua một cuộc khủng hoảng năng lượng trầm trọng giống như cố gắng xây nhà trên nền đất lún, nơi mọi công việc thường nhật đều trở thành thử thách đầy ức chế. Làm thế nào bạn có thể chuẩn bị tốt hơn cho hộ gia đình trước những gián đoạn bất ngờ về dịch vụ công ích? [p:Thiết lập một lịch trình sinh hoạt linh hoạt] có thể giúp bạn thích ứng khi hạ tầng sụp đổ.

en: Identify a critical utility in your area prone to failures and list three ways it affects your daily routine.
Prepare an emergency kit with basic supplies like battery-powered lights and a portable fan for sudden outages.
Establish a flexible daily schedule that allows you to shift essential tasks to hours when services are stable.
vi: Xác định một dịch vụ thiết yếu tại khu vực của bạn dễ gặp sự cố và liệt kê ba cách nó ảnh hưởng đến sinh hoạt hàng ngày.
Chuẩn bị một bộ dụng cụ khẩn cấp với các vật dụng cơ bản như đèn pin chạy bằng pin và quạt cầm tay để dùng khi mất điện đột xuất.
Thiết lập một lịch trình hàng ngày linh hoạt cho phép bạn dời các công việc quan trọng sang những giờ dịch vụ ổn định.
